extracted.intended_audience: media researchers, journalists, news editors, and social scientists studying broadcast news bias
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and auditing bias in television news selection and presentation using the Glasgow Media Group's 'Bad News' coding methodology; includes metrics for sources, framing, visuals, terminology, and comparison to independent statistics. Useful for content-analytic studies and for benchmarking story/headline selection on news homepages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source Asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial-dispute coverage allotted dramatically more speaking time to managers/government than to union representatives, even controlling for actor relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count and compare the number and types of sources appearing in a story (e.g., managers, government officials, union reps, grassroots actors). Measure both frequency of appearance and share of speaking time per source-type. Control for actor relevance (e.g., role in the event) when interpreting asymmetries; large disproportion indicates systematic privileging of institutional perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaking Time
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative measure of how much airtime each source or source-type receives within news bulletins or individual stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time and sum spoken words/seconds attributed to each identified speaker or category. Use speaking-time shares to assess dominance. Compare speaking-time allocations across actor categories and against expectations given actor relevance or objective involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story Selection (Selection Bias in Strike Coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some industries are over-covered relative to actual strike days; others under-covered, even with comparable disruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare frequency of stories on particular types of events (e.g., strikes by industry) to independent baseline statistics (e.g., actual strike-days, industrial action logs). Identify over- and under-representation by computing coverage rates per unit of real-world incidence. Use statistical controls for size/impact where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disruption Frame for Strikes
rubrics_metrics.description: Strikes are covered as 'disruption to the economy/public' rather than as labor grievances; this framing narrows newsworthy angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code opening sentences, ledes, and dominant frames for whether a story foregrounds disruption (to traffic, economy, public services) versus causes, grievances, or worker perspectives. Note whether the frame centers effects on non-elite actors (public inconvenience, business costs) rather than origins or structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Coding Bias (Visual Treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Camera angles, music, lower-thirds systematically present strikers unfavorably (workers shouting at cameras vs. managers speaking calmly behind desks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze visuals: camera distance/angle, shot selection, edits, music, lower-third text, and imagery used for different actor-types. Code whether visual choices convey calm/authority (e.g., podium shots) or chaos/aggression (e.g., crowd shouting). Use these codes to assess whether visuals systematically disadvantage certain groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic Asymmetries (Terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Workers' actions described with stronger verbs ('demand,' 'threaten'), management actions with neutral verbs ('offer,' 'respond').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code verbs, adjectives, and nominalizations used to describe actions by different actors. Track frequency of emotive/pejorative versus neutral/ameliorative language. Compare language used for similar actions by different actor-types to detect consistent asymmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical Distortion
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics about strike costs are prominently reported; statistics about wage erosion or workplace injury are under-reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventory quantitative claims and statistics presented in coverage; classify them by topic (e.g., cost-to-business, cost-to-public, wage trends, injury rates). Measure prominence (headline, lede, graphic) and frequency. Assess balance by comparing which types of numbers are highlighted versus omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-strike Cause Omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike stories typically opened mid-conflict, omitting the originating disputes — implicitly framing strikes as unprovoked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check story timelines for inclusion of background/causal information: does the story explain preceding events, grievances, or negotiations? Code presence/absence and placement (lede vs. body). Frequent omission of origins indicates a framing that portrays action as spontaneous disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disruption Premium (News-Value Implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that disrupt normal economic/social order are highly newsworthy when the disruptors are non-elite; the 'disruption frame' itself constitutes news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing newsworthiness or selection rules, account for an implicit premium applied to disruptive events. Operationalize by measuring selection likelihood conditional on disruption indicators and on actor social status; a higher selection probability for disruptive acts by non-elites signals a disruption premium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric Source Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Spokespersons of established institutions are systematically more newsworthy than spokespersons of insurgent groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code editorial decisions that privilege institutional spokespeople: who is approached for comment, whose statements are led with, who is given headline attribution. Quantify differences in placement (headline/lede vs. later in story) and repetition across bulletins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual-Friendly Bias (Selection for Packageability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories admitting calm, authoritative visuals (officials at podiums) are easier to package than stories requiring chaotic crowd visuals; selection skews accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate story selection against 'packageability' criteria: availability of neat visuals, easy soundbites, and authoritative figures. Compare selection rates for events with readily usable visuals versus those requiring messy crowd footage to detect bias toward visually-friendly stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-Centric Framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic stories are framed in cost-to-business / cost-to-public terms rather than benefit-to-affected-group terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code story frames for whether economic impacts are presented primarily as costs (to firms, economy, consumers) or as benefits/justice for affected groups (workers, communities). Measure headline/lede emphasis and placement of alternative framings; repeated cost-centric framing indicates systematic bias in value lenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: GMG Coding Scheme (Audit Methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Glasgow Media Group's coding scheme — source counts, speaking time, terminology, visual coding, story selection, and comparison to independent statistics — is a standard methodology for measuring structural bias in broadcast news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an audit, implement a reproducible coding protocol including: identify and classify sources; measure speaking time; code ledes/frames and terminology; code visual elements; record story occurrence and compare to independent baseline statistics; document coding rules and intercoder reliability. Use these components as benchmark metrics for content-analysis studies and for operationalizing checks on homepage/headline selection.
